title: Copies Near You
objective: After this level you can explain why popular videos and pages are copied to servers close to viewers, and what that saves.
summary: Content delivery networks keep copies of popular files on servers near viewers. Netflix's Open Connect puts servers inside internet providers and fills them off-peak.

cards.headline: Why send the same video across an ocean a million times?
cards.body: Level 46 showed that distance costs time, however fast your plan. So the busiest services beat distance the obvious way: they keep copies of popular files close to the people who want them.

cards.headline: A network of copies
cards.body: A content delivery network, or CDN, is a group of servers spread across many locations. They store duplicate copies of data, and each request is answered by a server close to the person asking. The trips are shorter, so pages and videos arrive sooner, and because the work is spread out, a sudden crowd of visitors hurts less.

cards.headline: Netflix's version: servers inside your provider
cards.body: Netflix runs its own CDN, called Open Connect. It offers internet providers its own servers to install inside their networks, free to qualifying providers, keeping video close to viewers. Because Netflix can predict what people will watch and when, it copies most new content onto those servers during off-peak hours. By the time you press play, the show has usually made the long trip already.

cards.headline: Level 9's trick, city-sized
cards.body: This is the cache idea from Level 9 again. A processor keeps copies of data in a small, fast cache because programs ask for the same things over and over. A CDN keeps copies near viewers for the same reason: many people ask for the same page or video. Each Netflix server inside a provider also takes a large amount of traffic off the links between that provider and other networks.

cards.headline: Copies: placed nearby
learned: A CDN answers from servers close to you
Shorter trips mean less waiting and spread-out load
Netflix puts servers inside providers, filled off-peak

questions.prompt: What is a content delivery network (CDN)?

options.label: One giant central server that stores the whole web
options.rationale: A CDN is many servers, spread out.

options.label: A faster kind of cable laid under the sea
options.rationale: A CDN is about where copies are stored.

options.label: Servers in many places holding copies, answering from nearby
A browser setting that saves pages you visited
options.rationale: That's your browser's own storage, not a CDN.

questions.explanation: A CDN is a group of servers in many locations that store copies of data and answer each request from a server near the user.

questions.prompt: Why does Netflix copy most new content onto its servers during off-peak hours?

options.label: Its shows are only allowed online at night
It predicts what people will watch and loads it while networks are quiet
Servers can only store files that arrive at night
options.rationale: Storage works at any hour; timing is chosen.

options.label: Internet providers charge nothing for data sent at night
options.rationale: The reason given is predicting viewing, not a free rate.

questions.explanation: Netflix predicts what members will watch and when, so it fills its servers during off-peak hours, before viewers ask.

questions.prompt: A CDN and Level 9's processor cache work for the same reason. What is it?

options.label: Both make the internet's cables physically shorter
options.rationale: Neither changes cables; they keep copies nearby.

options.label: Both erase any data that nobody has asked for yet
options.rationale: They keep copies; they don't erase data.

options.label: Both store a copy of every file that exists
options.rationale: A cache is small; it holds what gets reused.

options.label: People ask for the same things again, so copies get reused

questions.explanation: Programs reuse the same data (locality of reference), and many viewers want the same files, so copies kept close pay off.
